e.t: This word means a herd: a group of animals gathered or moving together. It is a noun, so it names the animal group rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek deuterocanonical material, it occurs ten times, showing a recurring but specific word for animals considered collectively. Its exact reference—such as the animals involved—comes from the surrounding verse, but the central meaning remains a herd.

This Greek LXX adverb means “continually,” describing something that happens or remains ongoing rather than occurring only once. It expresses repeated or unbroken continuation, depending on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including Esther, Psalms, Isaiah, Wisdom, and Maccabees. Its central idea remains steady across these uses: an action, condition, or expectation continues over time. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun means “decency”: conduct marked by an appropriate sense of what is proper and respectable. It names a quality rather than an action, person, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains decency—the quality of behaving in a fitting and respectable way.

This Greek word means “capture”: to seize people or take them as prisoners. It is a verb describing an action, not the person captured or the place of captivity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 36 times, showing repeated use for the act of taking people in warfare or defeat. Its references extend from Genesis through 1 Maccabees, while its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

“Negate” is a verb meaning to deny, cancel, or make something ineffective. It describes an action that refuses to recognize a claim, command, decision, or effect as valid. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in 4 Maccabees, from 4 Maccabees 2:1 through 17:2. The word’s exact force in any one passage depends on what is being negated, but its central idea remains setting something aside or declaring it without effect.

This Greek LXX verb means “change”: to make something different, replace one thing with another, or undergo alteration. It can describe changing an object, arrangement, or condition rather than merely moving from one place to another. The word occurs 37 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in this corpus, so its basic sense appears across several kinds of passages. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being changed and the surrounding context.

Amarphal is a proper name referring to a person named Amarphal in the Greek Old Testament. The name is preserved as “Amarphal” rather than translated into a descriptive meaning. It occurs twice in the Greek text, both times in Genesis 14:1 and Genesis 14:9. Because no verse text or wider context is provided here, the name itself does not establish additional meaning beyond identifying this person. Its precise significance in either verse must be understood from the surrounding passage.

Amiel, also rendered Amil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies individual people in the Greek Old Testament, including people mentioned in Numbers, Joshua, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. The name occurs seven times in seven verses, all within the Old Testament portion of the Greek LXX. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the person being identified and the surrounding context, not from a general abstract meaning of the name.

Amnon is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. The name appears 35 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 29 verses, with most occurrences in 2 Samuel. It is especially prominent in the account involving David’s family, though the name itself simply identifies the person called Amnon. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Anam is a personal name, functioning as a proper noun rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:58. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided, the name itself can be explained clearly, but the person’s role and significance must be determined from that passage and its wider context.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something as “blasted by gales”—damaged, withered, or affected by powerful winds. It is a descriptive word rather than a name for the wind itself. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament, including several occurrences in Genesis 41 describing the damaged grain in Pharaoh’s dreams. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the thing being described and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “sound in answer” or “reply.” It describes responding to what someone has said, whether by answering aloud or giving a verbal response. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 12:18. Its basic sense is therefore the act of answering or replying, while the surrounding sentence determines the precise force of that response. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality.

This adjective describes someone who acts “without hesitation” and remains “untiring.” It presents steady, energetic action rather than reluctance, delay, or weariness. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Proverbs 6:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a person who does not hold back and does not quickly become exhausted. The word therefore highlights readiness and perseverance in carrying out an action.

ἄπνοος means “without breath; lifeless.” It is an adjective describing something that has no breath or living vitality, rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it appears once, at Wisdom 15:5. That single occurrence supports a focused meaning, but the surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what it describes there. The word’s central idea remains the absence of breath and the condition of being lifeless.

Arabōth, also written Aravoth, is a proper name for a place. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word but as a named location in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs ten times, in passages from Numbers through 2 Kings, including references in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, 2 Samuel, and 2 Kings. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Ariēli, also rendered Arili, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Numbers 26:26, identifying a particular person or family name in that passage. The name itself does not provide a broader definition beyond this personal designation. Its precise significance in Numbers 26:26 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to “rapacity” or “snatching”—taking something greedily or by force. It describes grasping behavior rather than a person or object itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs seven times across seven verses, including passages from Leviticus, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Nahum, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains forceful or greedy taking.

Asban, also rendered Azvan, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Genesis 36:26. The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide an additional lexical sense or explanation of its meaning. Its role is therefore to identify a particular person in the biblical record, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific context for that occurrence.

This adjective describes something that is “inconvenient” or “inexpedient”—something unsuitable, unhelpful, or not worth pursuing in a given situation. It points to a practical lack of usefulness rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Proverbs 32:20. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what is being called unsuitable there, but the word itself carries this clear sense of what does not serve a helpful or fitting purpose.

Achim is a proper name, rendered as “Achim” or “Akhim.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:35. The available information establishes the name’s form and use as a personal designation, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or his role. Its precise significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding biblical context.

Achitophel, also spelled Akhitofel, is a proper name referring to a person in the Old Testament Greek (LXX) text. It is a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. The name appears 20 times across 17 verses, chiefly in 2 Samuel and also in 1 Chronicles. Its role in any particular passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and account; the name itself identifies the individual. The LXX rendering consistently gives the name as “Achitophel.”

This Greek LXX noun means “eatage; meat”—food intended to be eaten. It refers to something used as nourishment rather than to an action or a person. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, including four occurrences in Job and one in 3 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is food, especially meat or edible provision.

Galgala is a proper place-name: it identifies a location rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 32 times, beginning in Joshua and continuing as far as 1 Maccabees. English translations commonly preserve the name as “Galgala,” so its meaning is chiefly geographical identification. The particular significance of Galgala in any passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

Gamarias is a proper name referring to a person named Gamarias. It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament text of Jeremiah, this name occurs twice, in Jeremiah 43:12 and Jeremiah 43:25. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its particular role in each passage must be understood from the context of those verses.

Gemna, also given as Yemna, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. It identifies a particular named entity in the Greek LXX. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Joshua 15:46. Because the available record does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its specific identity cannot be explained further here; its basic lexical function is simply that of a personal or place name.

Gophera, also rendered Gofera, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in 1 Samuel 13:17 and 1 Chronicles 4:14. The available wording identifies it simply as “Gophera; Gofera,” so its ordinary meaning is the name itself. The surrounding verse passages would be needed to explain whom or what the name identifies in each occurrence.

This word means “repeated” and describes doing or saying something again. As a verb in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it points to recurrence rather than a single action. It occurs 12 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages from Genesis, Samuel, Kings, Nehemiah, and Sirach. The basic idea remains simple: an action, statement, or event is done again. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being repeated and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “blow through,” describing movement through a place or opening. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Song of Songs. Its wording presents movement rather than a static object or quality: something blows through. The exact force of the image in any one verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “melt”: to become liquid or lose firmness under heat or force. It describes an action or process rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Habakkuk 3:6. The word’s exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the dissolving or softening of something that was previously firm.

This verb means to “pass through” or “spread.” It describes movement from one side or place to another, and it can also describe something extending or spreading. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 134 times, showing that it is used broadly for movement or extension across different passages. The precise force in any particular verse depends on what is moving or spreading and the surrounding sentence.

This word is a proper name identifying a person, rendered “Dositheos” or “Thositheos.” It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it functions as a personal designation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times: three times in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which person is intended in each occurrence.

This is a proper name, rendered in the Greek Old Testament as “Dōēk; Thik.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so its ordinary function is simply to name someone. The name occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing five times in 1 Samuel and once in Psalms. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a personal designation.

gl: pledge put into the hand: surety; security
d: pledge put into the hand: surety; security

e.t: This word refers to a pledge placed in someone’s hand—a surety or security given to guarantee an obligation. It can describe something a person commits as assurance for another person’s debt or responsibility. As a noun, it names that pledge or guarantee; its use may also function adjectivally in a phrase describing something connected with surety. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, in Proverbs and Sirach.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “compute” or “calculate”: to work out a number, amount, or total. It describes deliberate reckoning rather than a vague estimate. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 2 Kings. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains the careful figuring or accounting of something.

This verb means “set on fire”: it describes causing something to catch fire or burn. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:3. Because no verse text is provided, the reference identifies its only occurrence but does not by itself show what is being set on fire or why. Its basic idea is an action that ignites something, rather than a general word for heat or brightness.

This Greek LXX noun means “elephant,” referring to the large animal. It is used literally as a countable noun, including references to elephants in military settings and other descriptions. The word occurs five times in the LXX corpus: once in Ezekiel and four times in 1–2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the animal itself.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to “spit on.” It describes the physical act of directing saliva onto a person or object. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, thing, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers and Deuteronomy, showing a specific but plainly understandable action used in those passages. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

The word means “nineteen,” the number that comes after eighteen and before twenty. It is a number word, used to state a quantity rather than describe a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented by this entity, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 2:30. The available lexical meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain what quantity it identifies there.

This word means “sixty,” the number six multiplied by ten. It is an indeclinable number word, so it functions simply to state a quantity or count. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 69 times across 66 verses, including passages that give ages, family totals, military or tribal numbers, and other counted amounts. Its repeated use in these ordinary numerical settings shows that it carries a precise, literal value rather than a broad symbolic meaning by itself. The surrounding passage determines what is being counted.

The verb means “bring in besides,” describing an action of bringing something or someone in along with what is already present. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Judges 3:22. Because the word occurs only there and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding wording. Its central sense remains an added bringing-in.

This verb means “urge on”: to press or encourage someone to act or move forward. It describes active prompting rather than merely offering an idea or invitation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Genesis and Proverbs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains the same—moving someone toward action through insistence or encouragement.

Etebatha, also rendered Etevatha, is a proper name for a place in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament: twice in Numbers and once in Deuteronomy. Its precise location or significance is not established by the name alone and depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “hostility”—an attitude or condition of active unfriendly opposition toward another person. As a noun, it names hostility itself rather than describing an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 26:21. Its basic sense is therefore clear, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that hostility is expressed in that passage. This LXX word should be understood as a description of conflict or antagonism between parties.

Zabad, also rendered Zavath, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 10:27, and refers to an individual identified by that name. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily its function as a personal designation, not a general concept applied across different passages. The exact identity or role of the person named Zabad depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Zouza (also rendered Zuza) is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a word describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea; it functions as a personal name. In the LXX, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:37. The available lexical information gives the name itself, while the verse context would be needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

Zoob, also rendered Zoov, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Numbers 21:14. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not specify whether it refers to a person, place, or other named entity. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the verse context.

Thaen is a proper name: it identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:25. Because the available record gives only the name and no explanatory definition or surrounding verse text, its personal identity and significance cannot be specified further from this word alone. The name is rendered as “Thaen,” preserving it as a name rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive term.

This Greek LXX noun means “marvelling”—a response of wonder or amazement. It describes the experience of being struck by something remarkable, producing an attentive or astonished reaction. The word appears twice in the Greek deuterocanonical corpus, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central sense remains the act or state of marvelling. It names the response itself rather than the person or thing that causes the wonder.

This noun means a window: an opening in a wall or structure that allows light, air, or sight through. It is a concrete word for an architectural opening, used across the Greek Old Testament and related writings. The word occurs 33 times in the Greek LXX corpus, showing that it describes a familiar feature of houses, buildings, and other structures. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a window or similar opening.

Ierami is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:33. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the name itself identifies the person but does not establish further details about his identity, role, or significance. Its meaning is therefore best stated simply: Ierami, the name of a person mentioned in Ezra.

“Itan” is a proper name referring to a person named Itan rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 15:55. Since the surrounding verse text is not provided, nothing further about this person’s identity or role can be stated responsibly. The name itself functions as a personal designation, not as a word expressing a general spiritual or moral concept.

This word means “fast asleep; fall asleep.” As a verb, it describes entering sleep or being deeply asleep. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 24:33. Its basic sense concerns the physical condition of sleeping deeply, while the surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on falling asleep or remaining asleep. The word itself does not express a broader spiritual or emotional meaning apart from that ordinary sense.

This Greek LXX verb means to speak ill of someone—to abuse or use words against them in a harmful, insulting way. It describes verbal mistreatment rather than simply making a neutral statement. The word appears once in the Greek Septuagint corpus, in 4 Maccabees 9:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This noun means “sentence,” referring to a formal judicial decision or penalty pronounced against someone. It names the result of judgment rather than the act of judging itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 12:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a sentence issued in response to wrongdoing or judgment.

This Greek LXX verb means “overturn.” It describes the action of turning something over or bringing it down from its established position. The word is used across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, appearing 40 times in this Greek LXX corpus. Its basic sense remains focused on reversal or destruction of what has been standing or established, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is overturned.

This adjective means “of cedar,” describing something made from, belonging to, or associated with cedar. Cedar is a kind of tree whose wood is mentioned in the Greek Old Testament in descriptions of materials and objects. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing especially in passages connected with Leviticus and the building materials used for important structures. Its precise reference—whether to wood, an object, or another cedar-related feature—depends on the noun and surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “weep” or “cry.” It describes the outward expression of grief, distress, or sorrow through tears or loud lament. The word is used 127 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it can describe many kinds of crying rather than one particular emotion or situation. Its exact force in a verse depends on who is crying and what has caused the sorrow.

κοινωνία is a noun for “companionship” or “contribution.” It describes people sharing life, participation, or resources in a meaningful common bond. The central idea is having a share together, whether through close association or by contributing to a common matter. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, in Leviticus, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls more on companionship or on a shared contribution.

This Greek LXX verb means “maim” or “cut short.” It describes reducing something by cutting it, or leaving it incomplete or diminished. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 4:12, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the thing being described.

This noun refers to a lizard, a kind of small reptile. It is a straightforward creature-name rather than a word expressing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, in Leviticus 11:29. The word’s exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical meaning here is simply “lizard.”

This word is a proper name: “Kyprios” or “Kiprios.” It identifies a person or named figure rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 4:29. The available lexical meaning is limited to the name itself, so its precise referent must be identified from that passage’s surrounding text; the bare reference does not establish more.

Labd is a noun used as the name “Labd.” It appears once in the Greek Old Testament translation tradition, at Psalm 118:89. Because the available lexical information identifies the word only by this name and does not provide verse text or surrounding context, its specific identity or role cannot be described further here. The word should therefore be understood as a proper name or designation rather than as a general quality, action, or object. Its exact significance in Psalm 118:89 depends on the verse and its surrounding passage.

This noun means “receipt.” It refers to a receipt or acknowledgment connected with something received. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times, so it is used across several books rather than being limited to one passage. Its exact sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a receipt: something that records or represents what has been received.

Mabsar, also rendered Mavsar, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint text of the Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 1:53. Because it is a personal name and no surrounding verse text is provided here, its meaning is best understood as the identification of the person named, not as a general theological or descriptive term.

This word means “long-lived”. It describes someone or something whose life continues for a long time, emphasizing duration of life rather than a particular action or event. As an adjective, it gives this quality to a person or group. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Deuteronomy 4:40. The word’s basic sense is clear, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific application in that passage.

This noun means “gift; offering”—something presented or given. In the Greek Old Testament, it refers broadly to what is brought or presented, whether as a gift or an offering. The word occurs 17 times across 16 verses, so it is used more than once but remains relatively specific in its focus. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being presented and to whom, but the central idea is a gift or offering given by one party to another.

This Greek LXX adverb means “vainly” or “in vain,” describing an action done without useful result, proper purpose, or lasting effect. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, appearing once each in 1 Kings and Job and three times in Psalms. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “magnificent”—something marked by greatness, splendor, or impressive excellence. It can describe what is truly grand or extraordinary rather than ordinary or small. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears 13 times, including passages in Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Sirach, so it may describe either a great quality or something worthy of admiration, depending on the sentence. Its central sense remains the same: expressing magnificence or greatness.

gl: seedling; shoot taken off and planted
d: seedling; shoot taken off and planted

e.t: This noun means a seedling or a shoot taken from one plant and planted elsewhere. It refers to new growth that has been separated from its original source and established for continued growth. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Wisdom 4:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and cannot be determined from the word alone, but its basic image is a transplanted young plant.

This verb means to perceive—to recognize or grasp something with the mind. It describes the act of noticing, understanding, or discerning what is presented, rather than merely seeing it with the eyes. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 31 times, so it can describe mental awareness in a range of settings. Its exact emphasis in a particular verse depends on what is being perceived and the surrounding sentence.

This adjective means “lazy,” describing a person marked by unwillingness to act or work. It identifies a quality rather than an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 15 times, with most occurrences in Proverbs and three in Sirach, showing its repeated use in wisdom instruction. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense remains a description of laziness.

This word means “see”: to perceive something with the eyes or come to behold it. It is a verb describing the act of seeing, whether the object is a person, place, or other reality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 52 times across 51 verses, so it expresses a normal and recurring action rather than a rare technical idea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being seen and the surrounding passage.

This adverb describes an action carried out responsibly and devotedly. It adds the idea that something is done with faithful care, seriousness, and wholehearted commitment rather than casually or carelessly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 1 Kings and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the action and surrounding words, but its central sense remains a devoted and responsible manner of acting.

This word means “everywhere,” referring to all places rather than one particular location. It is an adverb, so it describes where something is found, happens, or applies. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 42:22. Its basic force is broad and comprehensive: no place is excluded within the statement being made. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is described as being everywhere.

gl: reign as if one were king; govern badly
d: reign as if one were king; govern badly

e.t: This verb means to reign as though one were king or to govern badly. It describes an act of ruling, with emphasis on improper or harmful governance rather than ordinary leadership. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament translation corpus, in 3 Maccabees 6:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning is governing in a kingly or wrongful manner.

This verb means to “sit constantly beside” or “attend constantly.” It describes remaining beside someone with steady attention, rather than merely appearing briefly or visiting once. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Proverbs, where the wording presents a continuing presence beside others. The word therefore emphasizes persistence and nearness: someone stays at another’s side and gives ongoing attention. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic idea is continual attendance or sitting beside someone.

This verb means “reside”: to live in a place or remain there as one’s dwelling. It describes residence itself, focusing on where someone lives rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 65 times, making it a recurring term for describing residence across that corpus. The surrounding verse determines the particular circumstances of the residence.

This adjective describes something surrounded or enclosed by a colonnade—a covered walkway or row of columns. Its central idea is architectural: the object stands within, or is bordered around, a structure made of columns. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, so it describes a specific kind of setting rather than a broad spiritual or emotional quality. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “blow,” especially describing wind in motion. It expresses the action of air moving or blowing rather than naming the wind itself. The word occurs three times in this Greek LXX corpus: once in Psalms and twice in Sirach. Its uses remain centered on the movement of wind, giving the word a straightforward physical meaning within these passages.

This Greek LXX verb means “lead toward” or “head toward,” describing movement in the direction of a person or place. It can refer to bringing someone or something forward, guiding them toward a destination, or moving toward it. The word appears 169 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its basic idea is broad and recurring rather than limited to one setting. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on who or what is being directed and where.

This word means “prophecy,” referring to a prophetic message or utterance. It is a noun used to name prophecy rather than the person who speaks it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, including passages in Chronicles, Ezra, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains prophecy: a spoken or written prophetic declaration.

This verb means to become callous or to harden. It describes a condition in which something loses softness or responsiveness and becomes hardened. As a verb, it expresses this action or change rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Job 17:7. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the idea of becoming callous or hard.

This word is a proper name, referring to Remman, also rendered Rhemman. It identifies a named figure or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general.
